newsitem.title: USA: U.S. agency defends itself against cell-phone critics.
newsitem.headline: U.S. agency defends itself against cell-phone critics.

text.p: The U.S. agency that eavesdrops on global communications defended itself Thursday against criticism that it is hurting industry efforts to develop technology to make new cellular phones more secure.
The comments come a day after scientists said they had uncovered a key flaw that lets a sophisticated eavesdropper figure out the number a caller dials on the new breed of digital cellular phones.

Numbers that can be identified include personal ID -- or PIN -- numbers used to access a bank account or activate a phone calling card, as well as credit card numbers that callers might punch into a cellular handset to make a transaction.
The scientists said their findings highlight the U.S. government's overly intrusive efforts to control cryptography out of concern the technology may fall into the wrong hands.
In a statement, however, the National Security Agency said it "had no role in the design or selection of the encryption" technology selected by an industry trade group for use in the new phones.
"NSA also had no role in the design or manufacture of the telephones themselves," said the statement.
The NSA did say that it provided the Telecommunications Industry Association with technical advice on whether the encryption technology could be exported under U.S. export regulations.
David Wagner, a graduate student at the University of California at Berkley who helped break the code, said the discovery is "symptomatic of broad underlying problems in the design process."
